# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XIV. MRS. HECTOR TWISS MAKES A CALL

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

John Ashdown set off on a unhurried walk toward home. Shortly after starting, his thoughts lingered briefly on Clementine, yet as he arrived at Fern Hollow, she had completely slipped his mind, replaced by contemplation over an aspect of German theology that Harriet had mentioned. Unaware of his surroundings, he traversed Fern Hollow. German theology proved far too compelling for the beauty of Fern Hollow to hold any sway over him. Arriving at the manse, he headed into his study and removed a massive book from the shelf so he could determine whether he or Harriet had held the correct view. He stayed absorbed in its complex arguments until the sun rose, uncovered a fresh line of inquiry, and chased it with relentless determination throughout the following week, entirely detached from society, his congregation, and his relatives. He engrossed himself in reading day and night; whenever Ida was not present to pull him away, he neglected to eat his meals; thoughts of Clementine or Harriet never crossed his mind again. Across the harbor, elderly Mrs. Ambrose became gravely ill and summoned him, yet the note remained ignored upon his desk, collecting dust. Though Mrs. Ambrose pulled through, she never pardoned his absence. A youthful bride and groom arrived at the manse seeking to wed, and Mr. Ashdown performed the ceremony with untidy hair, clad in carpet slippers and a washed-out dressing gown. Indeed, he commenced by reciting the burial rites for their benefit, progressing to the words “ashes to ashes and dust to dust” prior to faintly sensing that an error had occurred.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0000 }

“Dear me,” he remarked in a distracted manner, “that is peculiar—extremely peculiar.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0001 }

Filled with anxiety, the bride started weeping, while the bridegroom, who felt not even a bit of nervousness, chuckled.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0002 }

“If you please, sir, my belief is that you are burying us rather than marrying us,” he remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0003 }

“Pardon me,” Mr. Ashdown said, as though it was of little consequence. He found the marriage ceremony in the book and finished it, yet for all the days that followed, the bride felt as if she had not been truly wedded.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0004 }

Once more, he overlooked his prayer-meeting—yet that was of no consequence, since the night was rain-soaked and no one appeared. He could have overlooked his Sunday service as well had Mrs. Hector Twiss not prevented it. On Saturday afternoon, Aunt Martha entered and informed him that Mrs. Twiss was waiting in the parlour to speak with him. A sigh escaped Mr. Ashdown. Within the congregation of Glen St. Agnes church, Mrs. Twiss was the sole woman he thoroughly disliked. Regrettably, she possessed the greatest wealth, and Mr. Ashdown had been cautioned by his board of managers not to displease her. The subject of his stipend was a worldly affair that Mr. Ashdown rarely pondered; the managers, however, were more realistic. Furthermore, they possessed shrewdness. Avoidance of any talk of money did not prevent them from successfully implanting an idea in Mr. Ashdown’s thoughts that Mrs. Twiss must not be angered. Had this not been done, he probably would have dismissed her completely from his memory the moment Aunt Martha departed. Because of this situation, he folded over the page of his Ewald, feeling irritated, and walked across the hallway into the parlour.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0005 }

Mrs. Twiss sat upon the couch, surveying her surroundings with a expression of disdainful rejection.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0006 }

How disgraceful that room was! No curtains hung at the window. Grace and Ida had removed them the previous day for court trains in a play they were putting on and neglected to hang them back up, a fact Mrs. Twiss was unaware of, yet her condemnation of those windows could not have been more intense had she known. Cracked and torn blinds hung there. Crooked pictures adorned the walls; rugs sat askew; faded flowers filled the vases; dust gathered in piles—actual piles.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0007 }

“What are we coming to?” was the question Mrs. Twiss posed to herself, after which she pursed her unlovely lips.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0008 }

As she walked through the hall, Tobias and Rupert were yelling and sliding down the banisters. Unaware of her presence, they kept on yelling and sliding, which Mrs. Twiss felt sure they were doing deliberately. Grace’s pet rooster strolled through the hall, paused in the parlour doorway, and gazed at her. Disliking her appearance, it refrained from entering. Mrs. Twiss let out a disdainful sniff. It was a fine manse, to be sure, in which roosters walked around the halls and stared people down.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0009 }

“Shoo, there,” Mrs. Twiss commanded, thrusting her changeable-silk, flounced parasol in his direction.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0010 }

Adam was shooed away. Because he was an intelligent rooster, and since Mrs. Twiss had personally snapped the necks of a great deal of roosters over her fifty years, she appeared to be surrounded by the aura of an executioner. As the minister entered, Adam hurried through the hall.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0011 }

Footwear consisting of slippers and a dressing gown were still worn by Mr. Ashdown, whose dark hair still hung in unkempt locks across his high forehead. Nevertheless, he possessed the appearance of the gentleman he was; whereas Mrs. Hector Twiss, dressed in her silk gown, beplumed bonnet, kid gloves, and gold chain, appeared to be the vulgar, coarse-souled woman she was. The hostility of each other's personality was felt by both of them. While Mr. Ashdown recoiled, Mrs. Twiss prepared herself for battle. Her purpose in coming to the manse was to suggest a particular matter to the minister, a suggestion she intended to make without delay. She was about to bestow upon him a favor—a major favor—and informing him of it as quickly as possible was ideal. Having pondered it throughout the entire summer, she had finally reached a resolution. In the opinion of Mrs. Twiss, this was the only thing that counted. Whenever she settled on something, settled it remained. No one else was entitled to an opinion on the subject. Such had perpetually been her stance. Upon resolving to wed Hector Twiss, she wedded him, and that concluded the affair. The way it occurred was something Hector had never understood, but what difference did that make? Likewise in this instance—Mrs. Twiss had organized every detail to her own contentment. It was now merely a matter of notifying Mr. Ashdown.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0012 }

“Could you close that door, if you don't mind?” requested Mrs. Twiss, loosening her lips just a bit to speak, though her tone was harsh. “There is something crucial I must discuss, which is impossible with all that noise coming from the hallway.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0013 }

Submissively, Mr. Ashdown closed the door. Following that, he took a seat in front of Mrs. Twiss. He remained partially oblivious to her presence. The points made by Ewald were still being contested within his thoughts. This distance was detected by Mrs. Twiss, and it irritated her.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0014 }

“In a belligerent tone, she declared, “Mr. Ashdown, I am here to inform you of my choice to adopt Ida.””
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0015 }

“To—adopt—Ida!” blankly staring at her, Mr. Ashdown failed entirely to comprehend.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0016 }

“Indeed. My mind has been on this matter for a while now. Ever since my husband passed away, the thought of taking in a child has frequently crossed my mind. However, finding a fitting one appeared to be quite difficult. There are hardly any children that I would desire to bring into my household. Taking a home child—most likely some slum outcast—is something I would never consider. Furthermore, almost no other sort of child is ever available. Last autumn, a harbour fisherman passed away and left behind six children. An attempt was made to persuade me to take one, yet I quickly let them know that I entertained no thought of adopting such rubbish. A horse was stolen by their grandfather. On top of that, every one of them was a boy, whereas I desired a female child—a calm, dutiful girl whom I could raise to become a lady. Ida will fit my needs perfectly. Provided she receives proper care, she would be a pleasant child—completely unlike Grace. Adopting Grace is something I would not contemplate for a moment. However, I will adopt Ida and provide her with a fine home and raising, Mr. Ashdown, and provided her conduct is good, my entire fortune will be willed to her upon my death. In any event, not a single penny of it will go to any of my own family members; my mind is firmly made up about that. In truth, the thought of irritating them inspired my desire to take in a child as much as any other reason at the start. Ida will receive fine clothing, education, and instruction, Mr. Ashdown, and I will see that she gets lessons in music and painting, caring for her as though she were my very own.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0017 }

By this moment, Mr. Ashdown had become fully awake. A pale blush appeared on his pallid cheek, while a perilous gleam shone in his handsome dark eyes. Could this female, whose coarseness and awareness of wealth seeped from every part of her, really be requesting that he bestow Ida upon her—his precious, small, yearning Ida who possessed the very same dark-blue eyes as Cecilia—the youngster whom her expiring mother had hugged to her chest when the remaining youngsters had been escorted crying out of the chamber. Cecilia had held tightly to her infant right up to the moment when the doors of death had closed between them. Across the small dark head, her gaze had met her husband's.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0018 }

“Look after her well, John,” she had begged. “She is extremely small—and easily hurt. The rest are able to battle for themselves—however, she will be wounded by the world. Oh, John, I am uncertain how you and she will manage. The two of you require me to such a degree. Nevertheless, hold her near to you—hold her near to you.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0019 }

Except for a handful of unerasable phrases meant solely for him, these had been practically her final statements. Yet Mrs. Twiss had unfeelingly declared that she planned to remove this very child from his care. Straightening his posture, he gazed at Mrs. Twiss. Regardless of his tattered slippers and threadbare dressing gown, an aspect of his presence compelled Mrs. Twiss to experience a slight touch of that former veneration for “the cloth” instilled in her youth. Ultimately, a distinct aura of sacredness surrounded a clergyman, even one who was impoverished, impractical, and preoccupied.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0020 }

“Mrs. Twiss, I am grateful for your good intentions,” Mr. Ashdown said with a courteousness that was gentle, decisive, and entirely terrifying, “nevertheless, my child cannot be given to you.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0021 }

Mrs. Twiss’s expression was uncomprehending. His refusal was something she had not ever imagined.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0022 }

“Why, Mr. Ashdown,” she uttered, amazed. “You are surely cr—this cannot be your intention. It is necessary that you reconsider—reflect upon every benefit I am able to offer her.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0023 }

“Mrs. Twiss, thinking it over is unnecessary. The matter is completely impossible. Whatever earthly benefits you are capable of granting her could never make up for being deprived of a father’s affection and guidance. Once more, I offer my thanks—however, it cannot be considered.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0024 }

Her customary self-restraint was overwhelmed by the rage of her letdown. Mrs. Twiss’s wide, ruddy visage flushed dark violet, and she spoke with a shaking tone.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0025 }

“I assumed you would be more than happy to give her to me,” she sneered.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0026 }

“What made you believe that?” Mr. Ashdown inquired softly.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0027 }

“Since no one ever believed you had any regard for any of your offspring,” Mrs. Twiss shot back disdainfully. “Your disregard of them is disgraceful. Everyone in town is talking about it. Their nourishment and attire are inadequate, and they receive zero discipline. A band of untamed savages possesses just as much politeness as they do. Performing your fatherly obligations never enters your mind. You permitted an unfamiliar youngster to stay with them for two weeks without paying her the slightest attention—a kid who used the language of a soldier from what I hear. It would not have bothered you if she had infected them with small-pox. Furthermore, Grace publicly humiliated herself by standing up to deliver a sermon and giving that address! On top of that, she traveled on a swine through the town—directly in front of your own face as I comprehend it. Their behavior exceeds credibility, yet you do not raise a hand to halt their conduct or attempt to instruct them in any way. Now, after I provide one of them with a fine residence and favorable future possibilities, you decline the proposal and affront me. What a splendid parent you are, speaking about cherishing and watching over your children!”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0028 }

“That will suffice, woman!” Mr. Ashdown said. Rising to his feet, he gazed at Mrs. Twiss with an expression that caused her to shrink back. “That will suffice,” he said again. “I wish to listen to nothing further, Mrs. Twiss. You have spoken excessively. Perhaps I have been negligent regarding certain aspects of my parental responsibility, yet you are not the one to bring it to my attention using the words you employed. We shall bid each other good afternoon.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0029 }

Mrs. Twiss failed to utter anything even remotely as pleasant as good afternoon, yet she made her exit. While she moved grandly past the clergyman, a big, chubby toad, which Rupert had hidden beneath the couch, leaped forth right beneath her feet. Mrs. Twiss uttered a scream, and while attempting to keep from stepping upon the terrible creature, she surrendered her equilibrium and her sunshade. She failed to go down completely, yet she stumbled and swayed through the room in a most unseemly manner, coming to a halt against the door with a impact that shook her whole body. Mr. Ashdown, having missed seeing the toad, speculated whether she was suffering from some type of stroke or fit, and hurried in fright to help her. However, Mrs. Twiss, regaining her footing, angrily motioned for him to stay away.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0030 }

“Do not presume to lay a finger on me,” she nearly yelled. “I assume this is yet another piece of your children’s mischief. No respectable woman belongs in a location like this. Hand over my umbrella and allow my departure. Never again will I step foot inside your church or your manse.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0031 }

Mr. Ashdown submissively gathered up the splendid parasol and handed it to her. Mrs. Twiss grabbed it and strode away outside. Tobias and Rupert had stopped sliding down the banister and were perched alongside Grace on the veranda's edge. Regrettably, the trio was belting out “There’ll be a hot time in the old town to-night” as loudly as their vigorous young lungs allowed. Mrs. Twiss convinced herself that the tune was directed exclusively at her. Pausing, she brandished her parasol toward them.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0032 }

“The father who raised you lacks any sense,” she remarked, “and the three of you are little scoundrels who deserve a thrashing that stops just short of killing you.”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0033 }

“He is not,” Grace exclaimed. “We are not,” exclaimed the boys. Mrs. Twiss, however, had departed.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0034 }

“My word, she is certainly insane!” Tobias remarked. “Also, what does ‘varmint’ actually mean?”
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0035 }

For several minutes, John Ashdown walked back and forth in the parlour, after which he returned to his study to sit down. However, he failed to go back to his German theology. He was far too deeply troubled to do so. Mrs. Twiss had stirred him awake with a vengeance. Could he really be the negligent, heedless father she had charged him with being? Had he truly so shockingly disregarded the physical and spiritual well-being of the four young motherless children relying on him? Were his parishioners discussing the matter as severely as Mrs. Twiss had asserted? It had to be true, because Mrs. Twiss had arrived to request Ida under the complete and certain conviction that he would surrender the child to her just as indifferently and pleased as someone might surrender a wandering, unwanted kitten. And, if this was true, what was to follow?
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0036 }

A groan escaped John Ashdown as he restarted his walking back and forth across the untidy, dust-covered room. What course was open to him? His affection for his children was as profound as that of any father, and no effort by Mrs. Twiss or others of her type could alter his certainty that their devotion to him was equally deep. Yet was he suited to be responsible for them? Nobody understood his own shortcomings and boundaries better than he did. The situation required the guidance, sensible nature, and attendance of a fine woman. Still, in what manner could this be brought about? Supposing he managed to hire that sort of housekeeper, Aunt Martha would be deeply hurt. In her own mind, she was still capable of performing every required and fitting task. He was unable to inflict such pain and offense upon the needy elderly woman who had shown such goodness to him and his family. Her devotion to Cecilia had been so great! Furthermore, Cecilia had requested that he show great thoughtfulness toward Aunt Martha. Indeed, a sudden recollection came to him that Aunt Martha had previously suggested he should take a second wife. He sensed that a wife would not offend her in the way a housekeeper would. Nevertheless, that remained impossible. Marriage was not his desire—he possessed no affection for anyone, nor could he develop it. What option remained for him then? The thought abruptly struck him to travel to Hollowmere so he could discuss his troubles with Mrs. Carrow. Mrs. Carrow belonged to that small group of women in whose company he never experienced shyness or a loss for words. Her nature was constantly so understanding and invigorating. There was a chance she might propose a remedy for his troubles. Even if that proved impossible, Mr. Ashdown was aware of his need for a bit of proper human company following his encounter with Mrs. Twiss—an experience to remove her lingering flavor from his spirit.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0037 }

He put on his clothes in a rush and consumed his evening meal with fewer distractions than he normally had. The thought struck him that the food was mediocre. He inspected his offspring; their complexions were rosy and they appeared sufficiently robust—with the exception of Ida, who had not possessed much strength even during her mother’s lifetime. The whole group was giggling and chatting—indubitably, they appeared joyful. Rupert felt particularly joyful on account of two exceedingly lovely spiders traversing the area around his dinner plate. Their tones were agreeable, their etiquette appeared acceptable, and they showed thoughtfulness and kindness toward each other. Nevertheless, Mrs. Twiss had stated that the way they acted was being discussed by the entire congregation.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0038 }

When Mr. Ashdown passed through his gate, Dr. Carrow and Mrs. Carrow rode by on the highway heading toward Kettlebridge. A disappointed look crossed the clergyman's face. Since Mrs. Carrow was leaving, traveling to Hollowmere would be pointless. Yet his desire for some company was stronger than ever. Looking out over the countryside with a feeling of despair, the rays of the setting sun caught a windowpane of the former Ainslie house situated on the hill. It gleamed with a rosy glow like a signal of optimism. Clementine and Harriet Ainslie came unexpectedly to his mind. He reflected that he would enjoy hearing a bit of Harriet's sharp talk. He reflected that it would be delightful to behold Clementine's gentle, unhurried smile and serene, celestial blue eyes once more. How did that ancient poem by Sir Philip Sidney go?—“continual comfort in a face”—those words described her perfectly. Furthermore, he was in need of solace. What reason was there not to pay them a visit? He recalled Harriet requesting that he drop by occasionally, plus he had Clementine's volume to return—it was proper to return it prior to forgetting. He possessed a troubling thought that his study contained numerous volumes he had taken on loan on various occasions and from different locations, failing to return them. It was certainly his obligation to ensure he avoided doing so on this occasion. Re-entering his study, he retrieved the volume, and descended into Fern Hollow.
{: #nw-v05-c14-p0039 }
